fields.meta_title: Community Landing Page Builder With Join Forms | Emergent
fields.meta_description: Build a community landing page from a prompt. See examples that sort each new member into a group or count event seats. Free to start.
fields.h1: Build a Community Landing Page That Routes Every New Joiner
fields.hero_description: Build a community landing page that asks one join question and sends each new member the next step that fits.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Behind the Join Button
fields.features_subheading: Emergent builds the community landing page and its join form; the app files each new name with the answer that sends them on.
fields.feature_1:
A page that says who the group is for

Describe the people you gather and what a normal week looks like. Emergent builds a community landing page from that prompt, and you change any section by prompting again.
fields.feature_2:
One join question that sorts people

Ask the question that decides where a newcomer goes, such as a running pace or a home city. The app saves the answer with the signup and uses it to pick the next step.
fields.feature_3:
Every joiner in a database you own

Each signup lands in a database you own, with the join answer and the date they joined. Sort it by group, or hand the whole list to the next organizer when the role changes.
fields.feature_4:
An alert to the organizer on duty

Name who welcomes each kind of joiner, such as a chapter lead or a ride captain. The app sends that person a Slack message or an email with the new name and the answer they gave.
fields.feature_5:
Linked to the tools you already use

The app connects to any tool with an API, such as Slack or HubSpot. New joiners can flow straight into the email list you already send from, with nobody retyping a single name.
fields.feature_6:
On your domain, code yours to keep

Publish the page on the group's own domain; custom domains are included in Emergent and use credits. On paid plans, export the full code to your own GitHub repository.

fields.tab_content_1:
Runners pick their pace once, on the join form

Riverbend Run Club's join form asks one question: the pace a runner holds for a mile. The app puts each runner in the 8-minute, 10-minute, or 12-minute group and emails Saturday's details: 7:30 AM at Fenwick Trailhead. Of 26 runners who joined in October, 13 run with the 10-minute group, Marguerite Soto among them.
fields.tab_content_2:
A member's focus decides which digest arrives

Every analyst who joins The Query Loft picks one focus: SQL, dashboards, or careers. Each focus has its own weekly digest and its own day. Of 38 analysts who joined in October, 17 picked SQL, 12 picked dashboards, and 9 picked careers. Imani Walsh chose dashboards, and her first digest comes on Thursday.
fields.tab_content_3:
Every new Austin name lands with Ingrid Mathisen

Brightvale College alumni pick the chapter nearest them: Austin, Chicago, or Seattle. The app emails the new name to that chapter's lead, who sends the first hello. Of 44 alumni who joined in October, 21 picked Austin, 14 Chicago, and 9 Seattle. When Rafael Ibarra picked Austin, chapter lead Ingrid Mathisen got the email.
fields.tab_content_4:
RSVPs shrink a seat count every visitor can see

Game night at the Long Table Board Game Club seats 40, and the page shows how many seats are left. Each RSVP takes one, and the app emails the guest a confirmation with the time and place: Saturday, November 14, 6:30 PM at Harbor Hall. With 33 of 40 seats taken, the page tells the next visitor that 7 are left.

fields.howto_title: How to Create a Community Landing Page
fields.howto_description: Follow seven steps to plan a community landing page around one join question, then publish it with a welcome that reaches each new member.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 Name who the group is for
fields.howto_step_1_des: Write one line a stranger could repeat: who gathers, where, and how often, such as new runners who meet on Saturday mornings. Every section of the page speaks to that person.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Describe what a member does in a usual week: the run, the thread, the meetup. Add two or three photos or quotes from current members, with their permission. A visitor should be able to picture showing up.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Choose the question whose answer decides where a newcomer goes next, such as their pace or their city. Ask for a name and an email besides that, and nothing more on the first visit to the page.
fields.howto_step_4_des: For each answer, write down what the new member should get and who sends it, such as the meeting details or a note from a chapter lead. That list becomes the routing in your prompt.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Describe the page in one prompt
fields.howto_step_5_des: Describe the page to Emergent in one prompt: who the group is for and what each answer to the join question sends. Emergent builds the page and the table of joiners, and you adjust either by prompting.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Connect the tools you already use
fields.howto_step_6_des: If the group already runs on a chat app or an email list, name it in your prompt. The finished app syncs each new joiner into that tool through its API, alongside the copy in your own table.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Join your own page, then publish
fields.howto_step_7_des: Join from a phone with a test email and check that the row lands in your table and the welcome arrives. Then publish on the group's domain and put the link where people already find you.

faq_plan.q: What is a community landing page?
faq_plan.a: A community landing page is a single page that tells a stranger who a group is for and what its members do together, then asks them to join. The best ones end in a short join form whose answer decides what the newcomer gets next, such as meeting details or an introduction to an organizer.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a community landing page?
faq_plan.a: Describe the group and the welcome each answer sends in one prompt to Emergent's AI landing page builder. It builds the page and a table of everyone who signs up. Join it yourself with a test email, check that the welcome arrives, then publish on your domain.

faq_plan.q: What should a community landing page include?
faq_plan.a: Include four things: who the group is for, what members do each week, proof from current members, and a join form. Put the next meeting or the next digest date near the button. A visitor who knows what joining leads to is more likely to click it. Save the rules and the group's history for the welcome email.

faq_plan.q: When should a community landing page sell paid access instead of a free signup?
faq_plan.a: Switch to a paid signup page when access itself is the product, such as a private forum or a monthly coaching call. At that point the page has to explain plans and billing, which is the job of a subscription landing page. A free group gets more joins from a form with no price on it.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should the join form on a community landing page ask?
faq_plan.a: Ask one question beyond name and email: the one whose answer decides where the newcomer goes next. Every extra field on a first visit is a reason to leave. Collect the rest later, in the welcome message or at the first event.

faq_plan.q: How can a community landing page show the group without exposing private posts?
faq_plan.a: Show it with material members agreed to share: a quote with a first name, a photo from a public event, or a summary of last month's topics. Ask before you use anyone's words or face. Counts work too, such as how many people came to the last meetup, and they reveal nothing personal.

faq_plan.q: How do I get more visitors to join from my community landing page?
faq_plan.a: Lead with the next concrete thing a visitor can join, such as Saturday's 7:30 AM run, instead of a mission statement. Put the join button above the fold and repeat it after the member quotes. Then test one change at a time, such as the headline, the way a high converting landing page is tested, and keep the version that brings more joins.

faq_plan.q: How can a community landing page welcome new members automatically?
faq_plan.a: Set the welcome by answer: each possible answer triggers its own email or message with the next step. A runner gets the meeting point, and an analyst gets the first digest date. With Emergent, the app can also alert the organizer who should say hello, by Slack or by email.

faq_plan.q: Can one community landing page serve several local chapters?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Add a chapter field to the join form and send each signup to that chapter's lead, and one page and one link then work for every city. When Emergent builds the page, each signup and its chapter go into a database you own. Count joins per chapter to see which city needs a second organizer.

faq_plan.q: Does a community that charges dues need more than a community landing page?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Once people pay dues, the page has to show tiers with their prices and say what each level includes. A membership landing page is built for that, renewals included. Keep a free community page simple: who it is for, when the next gathering is, and a one-question join form.

plan.angle: The SERP for this keyword is mixed gallery and platform content; none of it follows a visitor past the join button. This page shows four community landing pages built from a prompt and follows each join to where it goes: a run club that sorts new runners into pace groups and sends Saturday's meeting details, an online analytics community that routes each member to the weekly digest for the focus they picked, a college alumni network that alerts the right city chapter lead, and a board game club whose page counts seats down as RSVPs land. No tiers, dues, applications or renewals (those belong to the membership page): every community here is free to join, and the page's job is getting a stranger to the first run, digest or game night. The FAQ covers the definition, building one, what to put on the page, the join form question, showing activity without private posts, charging for access, getting visitors to join, welcoming members automatically, city chapters, and communities that collect dues.

The Query Loft asks each new analyst to pick one focus, SQL, dashboards, or careers, and each focus has its own weekly digest day (Tuesday, Thursday, Friday); of 38 who joined in October, 17 picked SQL, 12 dashboards, and 9 careers, and Imani Walsh's dashboards pick puts her first digest on Thursday.

Brightvale College's alumni page offers three chapters, Austin, Chicago, and Seattle, and a join emails that chapter's lead; 44 alumni joined in October, 21 Austin, 14 Chicago, and 9 Seattle, and when Rafael Ibarra picked Austin, chapter lead Ingrid Mathisen got the email.
